newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW - Canada seen nearer anti-Bre-X code.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Canada seen nearer anti-Bre-X code.

text.p: Canada would take about two years before it rectified the mineral reporting standards gap highlighted by the Bre-X Minerals Ltd gold scam, an Australian official in charge of mineral reporting standards said on Monday.
The Strathcona report on Bre-X's Busang samples had underlined suspicions held for years, Norman Miskelly, chairman of Australia's Joint Ore Reserves Committee, told Reuters.
"Absolutely, they're about to do it," Miskelly said when asked if Canada would tighten its mineral reporting standards.
"'Let the rivers run free' is no longer relevant in terms of Canadian financing for exploration south of the equator," he said.
He added that Canada would take some time to sort out its house on mineral reporting standards.
"It's been a pretty big kick to the guts (of the) Canadian mining, geoscientific and financing industries," he said. "They can't sweep it under the carpet anymore."
"I would suggest two years, something like that," he said.
The Bre-X case would have a long-term effect on the credibility of Canadian markets and its stockbroking industry, he said.

"We (Australia) went through this boom-and-bust situation 25 years ago. Canada is just going through it now," he said, noting that Canadian securities commissions had just established a mining task force to establish reporting standards.
The tilt would now move to quality stocks and to companies and countries that had established, responsible reporting standards, which Canada did not yet have, he said.
The investment market for speculative stocks, such as Bre-X,
would remain diffuclt for some time, Miskelly said.
The problem remained the fragmentation between Canadian provinces, interest groups and regulatory authorities.
"They want to reform it. They need a shot in the arm to make it actually happen. This is a catalyst," Miskelly said.

Old scams in the Australian mining industry, through cases such as the salting of nickel samples by Leopold Minerals decades ago, were effectively stopped 25 years ago by the introduction of the Joint Ore Reserves Code and the 1989 introduction of reporting standards, he said.
These became the model for world reporting and set standards which Canada should heed, he said.
""We recognise that we had a big problem here 25 years ago," he said. "We did something about it. Canada, chronologically speaking, is catching up or dragging behind us."

Miskelly also said that a Bre-X-type scam would not be allowed to continue for as long in Australia as it had occurred in Canada because Australian Stock Exchange officials and Australian analysts would work harder to extract the truth.
"Australian Stock Exchange officials would get in touch (with a company which had reported) to ask if its (reported results) are kosher," he said.
"Also Canadian analysts did not ask Bre-X. We (Australian analysts) are more sceptical, or cynical," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
